# Setup

Run this chunk first. If you don't already have the tidyverse, `require()` returns `FALSE` and the package is installed and then loaded. Otherwise it loads the package.

```{r setup}
#| message: false
if (!require("tidyverse")) {
  install.packages("tidyverse", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  library(tidyverse)
}
```

# Part 1: Quarto

A Quarto document (`.qmd`) has three parts:

1. A **YAML header** at the top (between the `---` lines) with settings like the title and output format.
2. **Text** written in Markdown.
3. **Code chunks** that run R code and show the results.

Click **Render** (or press Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K) to turn this file into an HTML page.

## Headings

Headings start with `#`. More `#`s give smaller headings. Note that you also need a space between the `#`s and the heading text.

### This is a level-3 heading

## Text formatting

This is **bold**. This is *italic*. This is `code`.

## Code chunks

Insert a new chunk with Ctrl/Cmd + Alt + I, or by typing three backticks followed by `{r}`. Chunk labels go after the `{r}`. For example, this chunk is labeled `basic-chunk`. The code chunk runs if you click the green triangle in the top right of the chunk. Next to this green triangle is a button which lets you run all chunks above it. The gear provides chunk options, letting you change whether code, output, messages, and/or warnings show up in the rendered document. Chunk options are written as lines starting with `#|` at the top of the chunk, like the `#| message: false` in the setup chunk.

```{r basic-chunk}
d <- 1 + 1
d
```

## Inline code

You can print variables directly in your text, like so: `r d`.\
This allows you to change your code without needing to update your descriptions or interpretations.

## Bonus: LaTeX math

Quarto can display math equations written in LaTeX. Put math between single dollar signs for inline math, like $x^2 + y^2 = z^2$, or between double dollar signs to display it on its own line:

$$
\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
$$

This is the formula for the mean (average) of $n$ numbers.

Some common pieces of LaTeX:

| Write this | To get |
|---------------------|:------------------:|
| `x^2`               | $x^2$              |
| `x_i`               | $x_i$              |
| `\frac{a}{b}`       | $\frac{a}{b}$      |
| `\sqrt{x}`          | $\sqrt{x}$         |
| `\sum_{i=1}^{n}`    | $\sum_{i=1}^{n}$   |
| `\alpha, \beta, \mu` | $\alpha, \beta, \mu$ |
| `\leq, \geq, \neq`  | $\leq, \geq, \neq$ |
| `\text{mass}`       | $\text{mass}$      |

Use curly braces `{}` to group things: `x^{10}` gives $x^{10}$, but `x^10` gives $x^10$.

LaTeX treats letters as variables and shows them in italics with extra spacing. To write ordinary words inside math, wrap them in `\text{}`: `BMI` gives $BMI$, but `\text{BMI}` gives $\text{BMI}$.

**Bonus exercise:** Write the formula for body mass index (BMI) as displayed math. BMI is mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

$$
\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{height}^2}
$$


# Part 2: dplyr

## Meet the data

We will use `starwars`, a dataset that comes with dplyr. Each row is a character from the Star Wars films.

```{r starwars-data}
starwars
```

## Function Basics

Functions take inputs (arguments) and return outputs. For example, `mean()` takes a vector of numbers and returns their average.

```{r mean-example}
mean(c(2, 4, 6))
```

**Exercise 2.1:** Use the `help()` function to see the documentation for `glimpse()`.

```{r ex2-1-help-glimpse}
#| eval: false
help(glimpse, package = "dplyr")
```

**Exercise 2.2:** Use the `glimpse()` function on `starwars` to see every column, its type, and its first few values.

```{r ex2-2-glimpse}
#| eval: false
glimpse(starwars)
```

## `select()`: choose columns

```{r help-select}
#| eval: false
help(select, package = "dplyr")
```

**Exercise 2.3:** Select the `name`, `species`, and `homeworld` columns.

```{r ex2-3-select-columns}
#| eval: false
select(starwars, name, species, homeworld)
```

**Exercise 2.4:** Select every column from `name` to `mass`. (Hint: `:`)

```{r ex2-4-select-range}
#| eval: false
select(starwars, name:mass)
```

**Exercise 2.5:** Select every column whose name ends with `"_color"`. (Hint: `ends_with()`)

```{r ex2-5-select-ends-with}
#| eval: false
select(starwars, ends_with("_color"))
```

**Exercise 2.6:** Select every column *except* `films`, `vehicles`, and `starships`. (Hint: `-`)

```{r ex2-6-select-except}
#| eval: false
select(starwars, -films, -vehicles, -starships)
```

## `all_of()` and `any_of()`: select columns from a list

Sometimes you already have a **character vector of column names**. Inside `select()`, `all_of()` and `any_of()` use that vector to choose columns.

- `all_of()` requires **every** named column to exist. If one is missing, it gives an error. Use it for required columns.
- `any_of()` selects the columns that **do** exist and skips missing names. Use it for optional columns or when datasets may differ.

**Exercise 2.7:** Select `name`, `height`, and `mass` using `all_of()`

```{r ex2-7-all-of}
#| eval: false
info <- c("name", "height", "mass")
select(starwars, all_of(info))
```

**Exercise 2.8:** You want to reuse a reporting script that sometimes receives a dataset with a `bmi` column and sometimes does not. Use `any_of()` to select whichever requested columns are available. Notice that `bmi` is skipped rather than causing an error.

```{r ex2-8-any-of}
#| eval: false
info_with_bmi <- c("name", "height", "mass", "bmi")
select(starwars, any_of(info_with_bmi))
```


## `filter()`: choose rows

```{r help-filter}
#| eval: false
help(filter, package = "dplyr")
```

**Exercise 2.9:** Keep only characters taller than 200 cm.

```{r ex2-9-filter-tall}
#| eval: false
filter(starwars, height > 200)
```

**Exercise 2.10:** Keep only characters whose species is `"Human"`. (Hint: use `==`, not `=`.)

```{r ex2-10-filter-human}
#| eval: false
filter(starwars, species == "Human")
```

**Exercise 2.11:** Keep only humans whose homeworld is `"Tatooine"`.

```{r ex2-11-filter-tatooine}
#| eval: false
filter(starwars, species == "Human" & homeworld == "Tatooine")
```

**Exercise 2.12:** Keep only characters with blue or yellow eyes. (Hint: `|` or `%in%`)

```{r ex2-12-filter-eyes}
#| eval: false
filter(starwars, eye_color == "blue" | eye_color == "yellow")
```

**Exercise 2.13:** Keep only characters whose mass is missing. (Hint: `is.na()`)

```{r ex2-13-filter-missing-mass}
#| eval: false
filter(starwars, is.na(mass))
```

## `mutate()`: create or change columns

```{r help-mutate}
#| eval: false
help(mutate, package = "dplyr")
```

**Exercise 2.14:** Add a column `height_m` with each character's height in metres.

```{r ex2-14-mutate-height-m}
#| eval: false
mutate(starwars, height_m = height / 100)
```

**Exercise 2.15:** Add a column `bmi` equal to mass divided by height in metres squared.

```{r ex2-15-mutate-bmi}
#| eval: false
mutate(starwars, bmi = mass / (height / 100)^2)
```

**Exercise 2.16:** Add a column `is_tall` that is `TRUE` when height is over 180 cm.

```{r ex2-16-mutate-is-tall}
#| eval: false
mutate(starwars, is_tall = height > 180)
```

## `mutate(across())`: change several columns at once

`mutate()` changes or creates columns. With `across()`, you can apply **the same function to multiple columns** without repeating the code for each one.

`mutate(across(columns, function))`:

- `columns` tells R which columns to change.
- `function` tells R what to do to each selected column.

**Exercise 2.17:** Round both `mass` and `birth_year` to integer

```{r ex2-17-mutate-and-across}
#| eval: false
mutate(starwars, across(c(mass, birth_year), \(x) round(x, digits = 0)))
```

*Brainstorm some other uses!*

## The pipe `|>`

The pipe takes whatever is on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right. You can read `|>` as "and then".

```{r pipe-example}
# These two lines do the same thing
head(starwars, 3)
starwars |> head(3)
```

Shortcut: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M. (In RStudio, turn on Tools > Global Options > Code > "Use native pipe operator" to get `|>` instead of `%>%` if you prefer.)

**Exercise 2.18:** Using one pipeline, keep only humans, add a `bmi` column, and keep only the `name`, `homeworld`, and `bmi` columns.

```{r ex2-18-pipeline}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  filter(species == "Human") |>
  mutate(bmi = mass / (height / 100)^2) |>
  select(name, homeworld, bmi)
```

# Bonus

If you finish early, try these.

**Exercise B.1:** Sort characters from tallest to shortest. (Hint: `arrange()` and `desc()`)

```{r exB-1-arrange}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  arrange(desc(height))
```

**Exercise B.2:** Count how many characters there are of each species. (Hint: `count()`)

```{r exB-2-count}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  count(species)
```

**Exercise B.3:** Find the average height for each species. (Hint: `group_by()` and `summarise()`, with `na.rm = TRUE`)

```{r exB-3-summarise}
#| eval: false
starwars |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_height = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE))
```
